Peter Van Breukelen/Redferns/Redferns hide caption toggle caption i Peter Van Breukelen/Redferns/Redferns Jack DeJohnette , one of the most daring and dynamic jazz drummers of the last 60 years, with a loose-limbed yet exacting beat that propelled a limitless range of adventurous music, died on Sunday at HealthAlliance Hospital in Kingston, N.Y. He was 83. The cause was congestive heart failure, Lydia DeJohnette, his wife and manager, tells NPR. DeJohnette had a singular voice at the drums: earthy and elastic, instantly recognizable. Rather than focus the articulation of tempo on his ride cymbal, he often distributed his emphasis around the drum set. He adapted this flowing approach from modern jazz innovators like Roy Haynes as well as avant-garde pioneers like Rashied Ali , devising what he called a multidirectional style. pages.text: Jaipur, India's Pink City, Turns 300 in 2027 | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD Why the Northern Indian City of Jaipur Is Brighter Than Ever This Year The Rajasthani capital wraps centuries of history and cultural tradition into one luminous metropolis. Rising up from the artificial lake of Man Sagar, Jal Mahal is a submerged pink sandstone palace built in 1699 as a royal retreat. Yukta Taneja By Arundhati Hazra Published October 20, 2026 The Pink City, as Jaipur is known for its colorful historic buildings, celebrates the 300th anniversary of its founding in 2027. Its majestic architecture ranges from imposing sandstone forts to elaborate palaces and colourful havelis—or heritage mansions—designed in a fusion of Indian and Islamic styles. Jaipur is also a cultural hub, home to centuries-old traditions of fabric printing and jewelry-making, as well as more recent ones, like the Jaipur Literature Festival , an annual event bringing together international authors. ( See all 25 of the destinations that made our list of the best places to visit in 2027. ) When to Go Jaipur’s subtropical climate and arid surroundings make fall and winter the best times of the year to visit. Between November and March, cooler temperatures and mild sunshine make it more comfortable to explore its forts and monuments. Several important festivals take place during this time, including as the Kite Festival in mid-January, when the skies are filled with a colorful sails, and Gangaur, a March harvest celebration that brings citywide processions and music and dance performances. pages.text: James Botham: Wales' unlikely hero in historic win over New Zealand - BBC Sport Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, James Botham was man of the match in Wales' historic win over New Zealand By Gareth Rhys Owen BBC Sport Wales Published 16 November 2026 James Botham lay sprawled on the Principality Stadium turf, pain and exhaustion etched across his face. Whenever the whistle blew, the Wales flanker in the red scrum cap took an age to rise. Precious seconds to recover. Nobody counts tackles when the ball is dead. But when play resumed, he was everywhere. Tackling, scrambling, hitting the deck and springing back up. By the final whistle, Botham had helped Wales beat New Zealand for the first time in 73 years. He was man of the match. And as the celebrations began, the tears flowed. Quite an afternoon for a player accustomed to working away from the spotlight. Keeping a Botham out of the headlines was always going to be difficult. His grandfather, Lord Ian Botham , is one of Britain's great sporting celebrities. Outspoken, charismatic and capable of turning cricket matches almost single-handedly, he is box-office. James is different. His game is built on tackles, chasing, wrestling and relentless graft. Few positions in rugby are less glamorous than blind-side flanker. But on Saturday, Wales' number six was the star of the show. DeWitt characterized people of Japanese ancestry during World War II. He insisted that even those who had been born and raised as U.S. citizens nevertheless posed a threat because their Japanese “racial strains” were “undiluted.” Under the authority of President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Executive Order 9066, DeWitt ordered the removal of all Japanese Americans from the West Coast in 1942. pages.title: Jesus de Miguel: Funeral of Tenerife forward takes place as family thankful for support - BBC Sport
pages.description: Jesus de Miguel's family say "the mark he has left on so many people" is something they will always remember as the footballer's funeral takes place in Spain.
pages.text: Jesus de Miguel: Funeral of Tenerife forward takes place as family thankful for support - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Jesus de Miguel's funeral took place in the town of Navahermosa in Spain on Thursday By Ben Collins BBC Sport journalist Published 5 November 2026 Jesus de Miguel's family said "the mark he has left on so many people" was something they would always remember as the footballer's funeral took place on Thursday. The Tenerife forward, who was 30, died after suffering a serious injury during a Spanish second division match on Monday. After colliding with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono, De Miguel lay motionless on the pitch while being treated by medical staff and was taken to hospital, where he died at 07:00 GMT on Tuesday. Owono was sent off for the challenge and the game was abandoned. De Miguel's funeral was held in his parents' hometown of Navahermosa, Toledo, about 125km from the Spanish capital Madrid. His Tenerife team-mates carried his coffin before the service at San Miguel Arcangel. Current Spain coach Luis de la Fuente was among the mourners, along with Real Madrid president Florentino Perez, Atletico Madrid chief executive Miguel Angel Gil Marin and former Real and Spain coach Jose Antonio Camacho. De Miguel's agent, Manuel Hernandez, issued a statement on behalf of the family, which read: "Thank you for loving him, for remembering him and for being with us. pages.description: Goalkeeper Jesus Owono will miss Equatorial Guinea's Afcon 2027 qualifiers after asking to be left out of the squad following the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
pages.text: Jesus de Miguel: Jesus Owono left out of Equatorial Guinea squad after death of Tenerife player - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Jesus Owono helped Equatorial Guinea to the quarter-finals of the 2021 Afcon but the National Thunder suffered a group-stage exit at the 2025 finals in Morocco Published 5 November 2026 Goalkeeper Jesus Owono will miss Equatorial Guinea's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers this month following the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel. De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday. Owono said he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" in a statement issued by his club FC Andorra on Wednesday, adding that it is "very hard to come to terms with what has happened". Equatorial Guinea's football federation (Feguifut) said that the 25-year-old had requested to be left out of coach Vincenzo Alberto Annese's squad. Feguifut president Venancio Tomas Micha had previously said his organisation was offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player. Owono has been first-choice keeper for the National Thunder since November 2020 and has featured at the past three Afcons. Equatorial Guinea face Zimbabwe in a double-header in Group E, with a home match in Bata on Thursday, 12 November before a trip to Harare four days later. The two teams sit level on three points after two rounds of matches, with DR Congo top of the standings on six points and Sierra Leone pointless at the bottom of the table. I spent two years mapping the areas surrounding one of the most beautiful drives in the world. Each morning, I looked forward to discovering and mapping an area adjacent to a one I did the day before. This diary entry serves as an introduction to a series of texts covering the challenges I encountered and how I overcame them. Included below are a few snapshots taken in the field, which capture the majestic landscapes along the Icefields Parkway. I have also added a “before and after” map excerpt, as well as a short video, to illustrate how my work gradually took shape over time. The Place The Icefields Parkway (Highway 93N), in Alberta, owes its name to the spectacular icefields and glaciers that line the road. The parkway, which is a 232 km stretch of highway cutting through Banff and Jasper National Parks, attracts between 1.2 million and 2 million visitors per year. The parkway offers exceptional alpine landscape, with glaciers, rivers, turquoise lakes, and breathtaking mountain views directly from the roadside (Figure 1). pages.text: JJ Gabriel transfer news: Real Madrid confident of signing Manchester United forward - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, JJ Gabriel joined Manchester United in 2022 By Simon Stone Manchester United reporter Published 4 November 2026 Real Madrid are confident of winning the race to sign Manchester United forward JJ Gabriel after reaching a verbal agreement with the teenager. The 16-year-old is registered at United, but has not been back to the club since walking out in September. Gabriel, who played against Atletico Madrid on United's pre-season tour, had been expected to become the club's youngest debutant in September's Carabao Cup tie against Brighton. However, he has opted to look elsewhere for senior football and has been training on his own in Spain. His availability alerted clubs around Europe, including Barcelona and Paris St-Germain, but Real now expect to sign the youngster in January. Though no club-to-club talks have been held, sources have told BBC Sport Real have verbally agreed a deal with Gabriel and his representatives. Gabriel, who scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut, has secured a European Union passport, which is expected to make it easier for him to sign for a club outside England. United would be due compensation should Gabriel leave, although the figure will be lower if he signs for a club outside the Premier League. He was named the Premier League's Under-18 player of the season last term, despite being only 14 when the season campaign. Participants may not know their fellow musicians, let alone the genre or dynamic, so there’s no choice but to embrace whatever the night brings. It’s about getting lost in music, together. Clouds move quickly across the Mackenzie Basin, dragging shadows over braided riverbeds and dry tussock plains that stretch towards New Zealand’s Southern Alps. One moment, the landscape is washed silver; the next, it disappears beneath a sweep of weather rolling over the mountains. I’m heading deeper into this high country on a window of borrowed time, crossing the 46,950-acre wilderness of Glenmore Station, a merino sheep, deer and cattle station. Hours earlier, the same storm front had grounded my helicopter flight to the country’s highest whisky bar — The Bad Decision, on a saddle above Glenmore Station — before it could leave the tarmac. pages.title: Journey Into a Prehistoric Cave That Trapped and Entombed Animals for Millennia
pages.description: The animals that plummeted 85 feet into Wyoming’s Natural Trap Cave provide a layered history of life dating back to the Pleistocene
pages.text: Journey Into a Prehistoric Cave That Trapped and Entombed Animals for Millennia Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Photos courtesy of Dr. Susumu Tomiya and public domain Natural Trap Cave is a pit in northern Wyoming into which countless animals have fallen and met their untimely demise since the Pleistocene. Paleontologists today find the cave a treasure trove — a stunning record of the species that have long roamed the area. The mammalian fossils left behind shed light on the climate, food sources and migration patterns of these species from earlier eras. Careful excavation work over the years that has involved sifting for bones, extracting ancient DNA, and looking for prehistoric pollen has revealed not just the plants and animals that once populated this part of the world, but also the ecosystems and climates that governed it. It also has required some rather advanced rappelling skills. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with vertebrate paleontologist Julie Meachen and Smithsonian contributing writer Michael Ray Taylor about what rappelling into Natural Trap Cave reveals about its contents and what it can tell us about Earth’s past. pages.text: JPR Williams: a revolutionary, a fighter and the ultimate competitor | Wales rugby union team | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation JPR Williams: a rugby union great who changed full-back role – video obituary Wales rugby union team This article is more than 2 years old JPR Williams: a revolutionary, a fighter and the ultimate competitor This article is more than 2 years old Paul Rees The foresight of a primary school teacher in Wales helped to create one of the best attacking full-backs of the 1970s Tue 9 Jan 2024 12.28 EST Last modified on Wed 10 Jan 2024 05.27 EST Share J PR Williams described himself as a diehard Corinthian, but he was also a revolutionary. When he made his debut for Wales against Scotland in 1969, it was in a position then regarded as the last line of defence. Only 15 tries had been scored by full-backs in major Test matches in 88 years, but the former British junior tennis champion changed the dynamic and smoothed the way for players such as Andy Irvine, Serge Blanco and John Gallagher. Williams, who qualified as an orthopaedic surgeon while playing for London Welsh, scored six tries in his 55 internationals for Wales, five against England, an opponent he boasted a 100% success rate against in 11 Tests. He was qualified to wear the white jersey as his mother, Margaret, was born in Rochdale, but there was never the remotest chance of a boy born and raised in the Bridgend area turning his back on his homeland. pages.text: Juan Mata: Former Spain midfielder retires aged 38 - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Mata celebrates winning Euro 2012 with Spain Published 18 November 2026 Former Spain midfielder Juan Mata has announced his retirement from playing at the age of 38. Mata, who made 41 international appearances, was part of the Spain squad that won the 2010 World Cup, and he helped his country win the European Championship two years later when he scored in the 4-0 final victory against Italy. A former Real Madrid youth player, he joined Valencia in 2007 before a move to Chelsea in August 2011 where he won the Champions League, Europa League and FA Cup. Mata moved to Manchester United in January 2014 and helped them claim the Europa League, FA Cup and League Cup prior to his departure in 2022. He went on to have spells at Turkish side Galatasaray and Vissel Kobe in Japan before he played for Australian sides Western Sydney Wanderers and Melbourne Victory. "Football will never leave my life," said Mata. "There are so many ways to continue loving the game, so many ways to keep using it as a vehicle for development. "I may stop playing professionally, but I will never stop being a footballer." Mata was Chelsea's player of the year in both full seasons he was at Stamford Bridge. He made 82 league appearances for the club, scoring 18 goals. "What a player," Chelsea posted on social media. That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race. The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris. But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances. Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business. This weekend, I was at State of the Map 2026, the international OpenStreetMap conference, which took place in Paris this year. Here’s a brief, personal feedback and a round-up of a few presentations that stood out for me. You can also find all the videos at https://peertube.openstreetmap.fr . NB: there is a French version here . This one was translated with the help of DeepL translate. The most inspiring: cartes.app Inspiring: cartes.app is a slightly mad project aimed at creating a new Google Maps, but without its car-centric bias. It started with a single contributor, but he’s managed to build a strong team around him: he has the insight to use the best open-source software components for his project – MapLibre for map navigation, vector tiles for map rendering, Photon for geocoding, and Transitious for public transport. Today, the developer is no longer working alone: he is securing funding and attracting contributors from around the world to improve his app and translate it so it can reach a global audience. It’s a wonderful project worth supporting, and you can do so by subscribing to cartes.app premium for just €1 a month. More Information The clocks developed by Ye and his colleagues are so precise that they would neither gain nor lose one second in 15 billion years, roughly the age of the universe. Atomic clocks are crucial to GPS and advanced communications, but Ye’s clocks can extend the applications to make precision measurements of gravity, motion, magnetic fields and many other quantities based on tiny changes in the atoms’ “ticking” rate between two energy levels. His group has set multiple records for accuracy and precision in atomic clocks and has made numerous advancements in optical frequency combs and ultrafast laser-based tools. Jungle: Tiny Desk Concert November 2, 2026 5:00 AM ET Robin Hilton Credit: Photo: Lexy Beale/NPR It's hard for any band to make the old sound completely new, but Jungle has spent much of the past decade transforming vintage soul and R&B into something almost alien. The grooves are deep and warmly familiar, with wistful reflections on love and longing. But even in the brightest moments, there's often a thread of mystery and melancholy that leaves you questioning whether everything is as it seems. Fronted by the trio of Tom McFarland, Josh Lloyd-Watson and Lydia Kitto, Jungle is known for fluid live sets, with songs that spill into each other. True to form, at the Tiny Desk, they perform more than a half-dozen tracks that run together in a single, continuous groove. "We're gonna keep the music rolling," Lloyd-Watson tells the NPR crowd as the band melts seamlessly from 2018's "Beat 54 (All Good Now)" into "Dominoes" from the 2023 album Volcano. The ONA was designated by Congress in 2008 for the preservation, protection and enhancement of seven key resources and values found on the site; these include the remarkable biodiversity and rich history of the site. The site is the only unit of the National Conservation Lands east of the Mississippi River, and the only unit managed by the BLM’s Eastern States. About The ONA is home a remarkable array of natural and cultural resources including four sensitive habitats, 26 special status species, and an archaeological record providing evidence of human occupation dating back over 5,000 years. These historic, cultural and natural resources serve as the bases on which the Congressional designation directs the protection, preservation and enhancement of the sites key values. pages.text: Jurassic period information and facts | National Geographic SCIENCE What is the Jurassic period and why did it end? The heyday of dinosaurs, the Jurassic era saw Earth’s climate change from hot and dry to humid and subtropical. The Jurassic period was characterized by a warm, wet climate that gave rise to lush vegetation and abundant life. Many new dinosaurs emerged—in great numbers. Above, Dimorphodon reptiles fly over a herd of Mamenchisaurus dinosaurs coming down to a river for a drink. Illustration by CoreyFord, Getty Images By National Geographic Staff Last updated August 18, 2025 The Jurassic is a geologic period that took place about 201.3 million years to 145 million years ago and constitutes the middle part of the Mesozoic era . The Jurassic period was named after the Jura limestone deposits in the Jura Mountains, discovered by German geologist Alexander von Humboldt . Building on this find, French scientist Alexandre Brongniart later coined the Jurassic period. There are three Jurassic time periods: early, middle, and late. Overall, the Jurassic gives us a particularly well-preserved fossil record of prehistoric life, which included theropod dinosaurs that scientists believe evolved to become birds . Thanks to this rich record, we know that the Jurassic was the age of dinosaurs roaming a tropical Earth filled with ferns, flowering plants, and conifers. It was also a time when sea monsters, sharks, and blood-red plankton filled inland seas borne of crumbling landmasses. Here’s what the Jurassic period was really like. pages.text: Jurgen Klopp says Fifa president Gianni Infantino worse than predecessor Sepp Blatter - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Jurgen Klopp took over as Germany head coach in July By Mandeep Sanghera BBC Sport journalist Published 16 November 2026 Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp says he "didn't think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that" as he called for Fifa president Gianni Infantino to be replaced. Blatter resigned as Fifa boss in 2015 amid a corruption scandal and was succeeded by Infantino in February 2016. Infantino plans to stand for re-election in March but has been under pressure since scrapping his Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, which included selling off stakes in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors. Infantino apologised to the Fifa Council for the plan but was told he was not fit to lead world football's governing body unless he released all the documents and answered key questions. "I've been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense," said former Liverpool boss Klopp. "I didn't think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that." Klopp added: "Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job." pages.text: Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) Skip Navigation Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) May 01, 2024 The Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) is a Census Bureau experimental data product that measures the economic and health outcomes of people who have been involved with the criminal justice system. Criminal justice involvement can include criminal charges, prison releases, and probation and parole sentences. Outcomes measured include employment, earnings, government program participation, and mortality. JOE is a collaboration between the U.S. Census Bureau and the University of Michigan that uses Criminal Justice Administrative Records System (CJARS) data to better understand how people involved in the justice system reintegrate into society. JOE covers criminal justice system involvement at any point between 2000 and 2020. Actual coverage of justice involvement depends on the coverage of agencies in the CJARS data, while coverage of outcomes depends on the availability of source data at the Census Bureau. Data users can download JOE data below or interact directly with the JOE data using the data visualization tool hosted by the University of Michigan. The tool includes additional justice-related outcomes created from CJARS without Census Bureau data. Experimental data products are innovative statistical products created using new data sources or methodologies that benefit data users in the absence of other relevant products. Justin Bis Justin Bis is the Chief of Staff for the Office of Technology Commercialization (OTC) at the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). In this role, he works alongside OTC leadership to maximize the impact of DOE’s investments in technology commercialization, strengthen coordination across the agency, and ensure long-term success. Mr. Bis has more than a decade of experience in government service and public life. He previously served at the White House as Special Assistant to President Trump and Deputy Director of the Presidential Personnel Office, where he managed the appointment of senior government officials responsible for regulating the U.S. financial and energy markets. At DOE, he was the Director of Intergovernmental and External Affairs under Secretary Dan Brouillette, serving as the department’s primary liaison to trade associations, labor unions, and state, local, and tribal governments. Beyond his federal service, Mr. Bis was the Executive Director of the Ohio Republican Party and Ohio Deputy State Director for the Donald J. Trump for President campaign. He holds a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from Northern Michigan University.
